title: Six Equations, Three Unknowns: from Bromberg to the Saxon Palace and back to an invoicing desk
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Bromberg, and the Change of Sovereignty

stops.name: Bydgoszcz, ul. Wileńska 6: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested (marian-rejewski.pl kalendarium; pl.wikipedia, both giving ul. Wileńska 6; MacTutor for the parents and the seventh-child position). Coordinate corrected: the research pool carried 53.1233/18.0006, about a kilometre south of the street; OSM geocodes ul. Wileńska, Bocianowo, Bydgoszcz to 53.1324/18.0004. No source reached this session fixes the individual building footprint.
stops.campa: In a town the German Empire calls Bromberg, on ul. Wileńska, a seventh child is born to Józef Rejewski, tobacco merchant, and Matylda née Thoms. They name him Marian Adam. The street signs are German, the schools are German, the administration is German, and the family is Polish, which under the Prussian partition is the ordinary arrangement. He will spend his first fourteen years a subject of the Kaiser, in a town that has not appeared on a Polish map for over a century. Nothing else about the day is recorded.
suggested_refs: The house at ul. Wileńska 6, Bydgoszcz, in the Bocianowo district

stops.name: Bydgoszcz, the Königliches Gymnasium: German lessons in a Polish town
stops.date_confidence: attested for the school and the 1923 leaving date (MacTutor). The entry year is inferred from the ordinary German gymnasium age and is not given in any source reached; month and day default to 01. Coordinate is an approximate central-Bydgoszcz placement of the historic gymnasium building, not resurveyed this session.
stops.campa: He enters the Königliches Gymnasium, where instruction is in German and the boys of Polish families learn it to the standard of the boys of German ones. In August 1914 the empire goes to war. In 1920 the town becomes Bydgoszcz and the school becomes a Polish state classical gymnasium, and the same pupils continue under a different flag with the same masters of Latin. Rejewski sits the Polish leaving examinations in 1923 and takes his certificate out of a school that has changed nationality underneath him. He reads and writes German to the standard of a native speaker.
suggested_refs: The Bydgoszcz classical gymnasium, formerly the Königliches Gymnasium of Bromberg

stops.name: Bydgoszcz, the death of Józef Rejewski
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 June 1921 by Wikipedia, 'Marian Rejewski', citing Polish biographical sources; not independently confirmed against a primary register this session. Pin is the family address on ul. Wileńska, not a confirmed place of death.
stops.campa: Józef Rejewski dies on the first of June, and the tobacco merchant's household is left to the widow and the children still at home. Marian is fifteen and in the middle of the gymnasium, in the second year of the Polish republic. What happens to the family's circumstances afterwards is not in the record: no inventory, no will, nothing beyond the date. He finishes the gymnasium two years later and goes south to Poznań, to read mathematics at a university four years old.
suggested_refs: Bydgoszcz civil registers for June 1921

stops.name: Poznań, the Faculty of Mathematics and Natural Sciences
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1923 (MacTutor); month and day default to 01 for the academic year. Coordinate corrected: the pool gave 52.4066/16.9310, about 800 m off; OSM places Zamek Cesarski, Święty Marcin 80/82 at 52.4080/16.9187, with the university's Collegium Minus immediately north. Krygowski's and Abramowicz's teaching of the first year is attested through Rejewski's own later letter, quoted by the Adam Mickiewicz University Press edition of his memoirs.
stops.campa: He enrols in the Faculty of Mathematics and Natural Sciences of the University of Poznań, founded in 1919 out of the wreck of a German royal academy and staffed by Poles who had spent their careers teaching in other people's languages. Zdzisław Krygowski runs the mathematics institute and Aleksander Abramowicz teaches beside him, and between them, in the first year, they put group theory and the theory of permutations into a nineteen-year-old's hands. Half a century later Rejewski will insist that he and his colleagues did nothing beyond applying what those two men gave them.
suggested_refs: Zdzisław Krygowski's mathematics institute at the University of Poznań
sources: Adam Mickiewicz University Press, edition page for Rejewski's Wspomnienia

stops.name: Poznań, the course held after hours
stops.date_confidence: start date 15 January 1929 attested (Wikipedia, 'Marian Rejewski'). Sources disagree on the course's end, 22 March against May; the pool could not resolve it, and it matters little here because Rejewski left before it concluded to take up the Göttingen scholarship (marian-rejewski.pl, giving summer 1929 to summer 1930 in Göttingen). Ciężki's role as one of the teachers follows MacTutor.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of January a small number of mathematics students, selected without being told the criterion, are called to the institute after hours. The Cipher Bureau of the General Staff has come from Poznań's garrison and from Warsaw looking for mathematicians who read German. Maksymilian Ciężki teaches part of it, the students swear secrecy, and the work is done in a locked room at night. Rejewski leaves before the course ends, his Göttingen scholarship having come through. Two others stay to the finish: Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski.
stops.quote: Well, one day or one evening, I don't remember which, one of the younger mathematics students came up to me and said that on such-and-such a day, at such-and-such an hour, Professor [Zdzisław] Krygowski [director of Poznań University's Mathematics Institute] wanted me to come to the Institute... In any case, not all the students were selected....
stops.quote_source: Marian Rejewski, in Richard Woytak, 'A Conversation with Marian Rejewski', Appendix B in Władysław Kozaczuk, Enigma (1984), p. 229, as quoted in Chris Christensen, Mathematics Magazine 80.4 (2007), p. 252. The long medial ellipsis is this file's elision; the shorter ones are Christensen's.
suggested_refs: The Cipher Bureau's 1929 cryptology course for Poznań mathematics students
sources: Chris Christensen, 'Polish Mathematicians Finding Patterns in Enigma Messages', Mathematics Magazine 80.4 (2007)

stops.name: Poznań, magister filozofii
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 March 1929, with the thesis subject, by MacTutor. That Poznań taught permutation groups more thoroughly than most Polish faculties is an inference from Krygowski's own field and from Rejewski's letter naming him and Abramowicz, not a claim any source makes in those words.
stops.campa: The degree of magister filozofii is awarded on the first of March for a thesis on the theory of doubly periodic functions of the second and third kinds: elliptic function theory, with no conceivable military application then or afterwards. What will matter lies elsewhere in the same curriculum, in the permutation groups of the first year. He is twenty-three, and has told nobody about the oath he swore in January. In the autumn he leaves for Germany on a scholarship in actuarial statistics.
suggested_refs: Rejewski's 1929 Poznań thesis on doubly periodic functions of the second and third kinds

stops.name: Göttingen, the year of actuarial statistics
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period (MacTutor; marian-rejewski.pl gives summer 1929 to summer 1930) but no exact arrival day is given in any reached source, so month and day are set to the start of the winter semester. The disappointment with the instruction is MacTutor's report of Rejewski's own view; nothing states which courses he means.
stops.campa: He spends a year at Göttingen on actuarial statistics, insurance mathematics, the branch a Polish mathematics graduate could actually be paid to practise. It is the Göttingen of Hilbert and Courant, the most famous mathematics faculty in the world. Rejewski comes away disappointed by the level of the instruction he received, which is either a verdict on the actuarial courses or on himself, and the record does not say which. He returns to Poznań in the summer of 1930 without a doctorate and without an insurance job.
suggested_refs: The Göttingen mathematics faculty in the last years before 1933

stops.name: Poznań, the assistantship and the cellar office
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1930 for both the assistantship under Krygowski (MacTutor) and the part-time Cipher Bureau outpost work (Wikipedia, 'Marian Rejewski'); month and day default to the start of the academic year. The twelve-hours-a-week figure and the cellar location are given by the Polish literature summarised in the pool and were not confirmed against a primary source this session.
stops.campa: Krygowski takes him on as an assistant in the mathematics institute. In the same season the Cipher Bureau opens a branch office in Poznań and quietly employs the graduates of its own secret course, part time, in a room below the military command, on ordinary German hand ciphers of the army and the administration. The men doing it go back upstairs afterwards to teach calculus. Rejewski holds both posts for two years. In the summer of 1932 the Poznań office is shut and its best people are moved to Warsaw.
suggested_refs: The Cipher Bureau's Poznań outpost, 1930-1932

segments.name: The Saxon Palace: Six Equations, Three Unknowns

stops.name: Warsaw, the Saxon Palace: section BS-4
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 September 1932 (Wikipedia, 'Marian Rejewski'; marian-rejewski.pl). Coordinate corrected: the pool gave 52.2436/21.0122, some 270 m north of the palace footprint in the Ogrod Saski block; OSM places plac Piłsudskiego, the Saxon Palace site, at 52.2412/21.0125. That linguists rather than mathematicians had previously run the section is the standard account in the literature and is not sourced to a document here.
stops.campa: He gives up the university post and joins the German section of the Cipher Bureau, BS-4, in the Saxon Palace on what is now Piłsudski Square. Różycki and Zygalski come with him. The bureau has held a commercial Enigma for years and has got nowhere with the military machine; so have the French, and so have the British, and the professional linguists who have run cryptanalysis since the last war have written the problem off as closed. The bureau's answer is to hire three mathematicians in their twenties and sit them at a desk.
suggested_refs: The Saxon Palace, plac Piłsudskiego, Warsaw, destroyed by German engineers in December 1944

stops.name: Warsaw, the photographs from Paris
stops.date_confidence: contradiction not resolved: Wikipedia gives 9-10 December 1932 for the handover of the French material, the research dossier gives 8 December citing Rejewski's own recollection, and Rejewski's published account as quoted by Christensen says 9 December. The 9th is used here because it is what the quoted primary text says, but the discrepancy stands. That he was assigned the machine alone in October 1932 is attested (Wikipedia).
stops.campa: In October he had been given the military Enigma to himself, in a separate room, and told to say nothing to the others. He works from the doubled message key, the six letters each operator enciphers twice at the head of a transmission, and writes the machine as a product of permutations. It resolves to six equations in three unknowns and stops there. On the ninth of December Gustave Bertrand's service in Paris passes over photographs of German daily key tables for September and October, bought from Hans-Thilo Schmidt of the Reich cipher office.
stops.quote: ...I had a set of six equations with three unknowns - S, N, and Q. And just as I was wondering how to solve this set, quite unexpectedly on 9 December 1932, at just the right moment, I was given a photocopy of two tables of daily keys for September and October 1932.
stops.quote_source: Marian Rejewski, 'How the Polish Mathematicians Broke Enigma', Appendix D in Kozaczuk, Enigma (1984), p. 256, as quoted in Christensen, Mathematics Magazine 80.4 (2007), p. 266
suggested_refs: Hans-Thilo Schmidt's documents, supplied to French intelligence from 1931
sources: Chris Christensen, 'Polish Mathematicians Finding Patterns in Enigma Messages', Mathematics Magazine 80.4 (2007)

stops.name: Warsaw, the last days of December
stops.date_confidence: attested to the final days of December 1932 (Wikipedia, 'Marian Rejewski'); no source reached gives a day, and the 28th is a placeholder within the attested window. The AVA works building Enigma doubles from the recovered wiring is standard in the literature and was not confirmed against a primary document here.
stops.campa: In the last days of December the wiring of the right-hand rotor falls out of the equations, then the reflector, then the rest of the machine. Intercepted traffic is fed to the reconstruction and the traffic reads. Rejewski has been on the problem alone since October, with the doubled key, a theorem on the product of transpositions and two months of German daily settings bought from a clerk in Berlin. The AVA works in Warsaw begins building doubles of a machine no Pole has ever seen, and nothing is announced.
stops.quote: Whenever there is arbitrariness, there is also a certain regularity. There is no avoiding it.
stops.quote_source: Marian Rejewski, in Richard Woytak, 'A Conversation with Marian Rejewski', Appendix B in Kozaczuk, Enigma (1984), p. 235, as quoted in Christensen, Mathematics Magazine 80.4 (2007), p. 247
suggested_refs: The AVA Radio Manufacturing Company, Warsaw, builder of the Polish Enigma doubles
sources: Chris Christensen, 'Polish Mathematicians Finding Patterns in Enigma Messages', Mathematics Magazine 80.4 (2007)

stops.name: Bydgoszcz, the Church of the Sacred Heart: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R] as to the church and the ceremony: marian-rejewski.pl gives the date and the Church of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, MacTutor gives the marriage and the bride's father's profession, and a 2022 popular biography was publicly criticised in Bydgoszcz for errors precisely about churches and addresses, so the venue is carried as unresolved. Coordinate is an approximate placement of the church in Bydgoszcz.
stops.campa: He marries Irena Maria Lewandowska, a dentist's daughter, in the town where both of them grew up. He is twenty-eight and cannot tell his wife what he does. What she is told, for the rest of the decade and through the war after it, is that her husband works for the General Staff. That is true, and it is the whole of what she is permitted. He has come up from Warsaw for the ceremony and goes back to the Saxon Palace afterwards. They take rooms in the capital on a second-department civil servant's salary.
suggested_refs: Parish registers of the Church of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, Bydgoszcz, June 1934

stops.name: Warsaw, ul. Zajączka 7: the household that is told nothing
stops.date_confidence: attested for summer 1934 and the address (marian-rejewski.pl); the same chronology lists ul. Sułkowskiego and ul. Mickiewicza 12 for the same year, and one address is used here to stand for three. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 52.2606/20.9764 to OSM's geocode of ul. Generała Józefa Zajączka, Stary Żoliborz, 52.2612/20.9859. Children's birth dates from Wikipedia; the cyclometer figure of 105,456 settings is standard in the literature.
stops.campa: The Rejewskis take a flat on ul. Zajączka in Żoliborz, one of three addresses the family chronology gives for that year. A son, Andrzej, is born in June 1936; a daughter, Janina, in February 1939. The father leaves in the morning for a building on Piłsudski Square, comes home in the evening, and says nothing about the day. In these same years he and Zygalski build the cyclometer, a machine for cataloguing the characteristics of all one hundred and five thousand four hundred and fifty-six rotor settings, a year of work at a hand crank.
suggested_refs: The cyclometer of Rejewski and Zygalski, and the card catalogue of rotor characteristics

stops.name: Warsaw, the second of November: the catalogue becomes waste paper
stops.date_confidence: attested in Rejewski's own published account, quoted verbatim below. Pin is the Cipher Bureau at the Saxon Palace; the bureau had by then also begun moving sensitive work to the Pyry installation, and no source reached states where the catalogue itself was kept on that date.
stops.campa: The card catalogue is finished after a year of grinding it out by hand. On the second of November the Germans exchange reflector A for reflector B, and every card in the catalogue becomes waste paper at once. Rejewski reconstructs the connections of the new drum, as he had reconstructed the connections of the old one five years earlier, and the team starts the catalogue over from the beginning. A year of labour is voided in a day and done again. In his own account of it, written decades afterwards, the whole episode gets one sentence.
stops.quote: Unfortunately, on 2 November 1937, when the card catalogue was ready, the Germans exchanged the reversing drum [reflector] that they had been using, which they designated by the letter A, for another drum, a B drum, and consequently, we had to do the whole job over again, after first reconstructing the connections in drum B, of course.
stops.quote_source: Marian Rejewski, 'How the Polish Mathematicians Broke Enigma', Appendix D in Kozaczuk, Enigma (1984), p. 264, as quoted in Christensen, Mathematics Magazine 80.4 (2007), p. 262
suggested_refs: The German exchange of Enigma reflector A for reflector B, 2 November 1937
sources: Chris Christensen, 'Polish Mathematicians Finding Patterns in Enigma Messages', Mathematics Magazine 80.4 (2007)

stops.name: Warsaw, the fifteenth of September: the indicator changes
stops.date_confidence: attested to 15 September 1938 (Wikipedia, 'Marian Rejewski'). The Gold Cross of Merit is attested for 1938 without a day (Wikipedia, cross-checked in the pool with Wojciech Polak's study of the security files) and is placed here rather than given a stop of its own. That the bomba and the Zygalski sheets followed within weeks is the standard account; no reached source dates either invention exactly.
stops.campa: The army and the air force change the indicator procedure. The operator now chooses his own ground setting for every message, and the doubled key on which the whole Polish method rested stops giving itself away in the old manner. Within weeks Rejewski designs the bomba, six Enigma doubles linked and driven through the rotor positions together, and Zygalski designs the perforated sheets. Earlier the same year the three of them had been decorated in secret; Rejewski received the Gold Cross of Merit. No citation accompanying it describes the work.
suggested_refs: The bomba kryptologiczna of 1938 and the Zygalski perforated sheets

segments.name: Pyry, and the Road to Kuty

stops.name: Pyry, the conference in the forest
stops.date_confidence: attested for 25-26 July 1939 (GCHQ, 'The Pyry Forest Meeting'); the Polish chronology gives a wider 24-27 July window and Denniston's own report emphasises the 26th. Alan Turing was not present, which GCHQ states explicitly. Coordinate corrected: the pool's 52.1370/21.0400 sits in the Kabaty forest well east of the site; OSM places Pyry, Ursynow, at 52.1315/21.0214. Knox's silence on the return journey is anecdote carried in the literature and is not attested by any source reached [R].
stops.campa: In a forest installation south of Warsaw the Cipher Bureau shows the French and the British what it has been holding. Alastair Denniston and Dilly Knox come from London, Gustave Bertrand from Paris. Rejewski, Różycki and Zygalski set out the permutation method, the bomba, the perforated sheets and the reconstructed rotor wiring. Knox has been working the machine for years and learns in an afternoon what he could not get out of it. Two Polish-built Enigma doubles are handed over, one to each delegation, and the delegations carry them home in the last week of July 1939.
stops.quote: A team led by Marian Rejewski worked out the wirings of the German Army Enigma rotors and had some early success by building replica Enigma machines
stops.quote_source: Sir Iain Lobban, Director of GCHQ, 2014 commemorative speech on the Pyry meeting, gchq.gov.uk
suggested_refs: The Pyry forest meeting of 25-26 July 1939 and the two Enigma doubles handed to the French and British delegations
sources: GCHQ, 'Director GCHQ commemorates crucial pre-war Enigma information sharing meeting'

stops.name: Warszawa Wileńska, the evacuation east
stops.date_confidence: attested to 5 September 1939 for the start of the Cipher Bureau evacuation (Wikipedia). The departure point is given by marian-rejewski.pl only as 'Warszawa Wileńska', and the pool could not establish whether that names the railway station or the district; the coordinate is the Wileńska station area. The family's move to Bydgoszcz is inferred from the 1946 reunion address and is not separately attested for 1939.
stops.campa: Four days into the invasion the Cipher Bureau burns its papers and goes east. Rejewski leaves from the Wileńska side of the river with the section's people and what equipment can be carried. He leaves behind a wife, a three-year-old son and a six-month-old daughter. He will not see any of them again for seven years and two months, and will not stand in Warsaw again for thirty. The column moves out through Mińsk Mazowiecki and Siedlce, on roads being strafed from the air.
suggested_refs: The Cipher Bureau evacuation route out of Warsaw, September 1939

stops.name: Kuty, the crossing into Romania
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Kuty crossing on 17 September 1939, the day of the Soviet invasion (marian-rejewski.pl; Wikipedia). The intermediate towns are all given by the same chronology as separate route points and are compressed here into one stop. The burial or destruction of the bomby near the border rests on a recovered Polish evacuation report cited by Borowiak and Grajek, which the pool could not refetch [R].
stops.campa: The route runs Brześć, Kowel, Łuck, Dubno, Tarnopol, Czortków, each an ordinary Polish town in the second week of September and none of them Polish by the third. On the seventeenth the Soviet Union invades from the east and the only remaining direction is south. At Kuty on the Czeremosz the Cipher Bureau crosses into Romania. According to the surviving evacuation report the bomby were destroyed or buried near the border. None has ever been found.
suggested_refs: The Kuty border crossing, 17 September 1939
Mariusz Borowiak and Marek Grajek on the fate of the Polish bomby

stops.name: Bucharest, the diplomatic quarter
stops.date_confidence: attested to 21 September 1939 (marian-rejewski.pl). Coordinate is a central-Bucharest approximation; the building used by the Polish mission was not identified this session. The onward route through Yugoslavia, Italy and Modane is from the same chronology.
stops.campa: The party reaches Bucharest on the twenty-first and goes to the Polish diplomatic mission, one more group of refugees among the tens of thousands the September evacuation has pushed over the Romanian border. Whatever is arranged there is arranged fast: within days Rejewski, Różycki and Zygalski are travelling west with papers, through Yugoslavia and Italy and the Modane tunnel into France. What the mission was told about the three of them, and by whom, is in no surviving account.
suggested_refs: The Polish diplomatic mission in Bucharest, September 1939

segments.name: Bruno and Cadix: the War Fought Under Other People's Flags

stops.name: Paris, the équipe reassembled
stops.date_confidence: attested to about 25 September 1939 (marian-rejewski.pl). Paris coordinate inherited byte-identical from the corpus standard used across existing journey files. The composition of the team, fifteen Poles and seven Spanish Republican cryptologists, is the figure carried in the literature on P.C. Bruno and was not verified against a primary document here.
stops.campa: He reaches Paris about the twenty-fifth of September, a month after leaving Warsaw. Gustave Bertrand, who supplied the German key tables in 1932 and sat in the forest at Pyry in July, now has the Polish team on French soil and a use for it. The Deuxième Bureau reassembles the section as the équipe Z: fifteen Poles and seven Spanish Republicans, under French command. The Polish government is at Angers and the Polish army is being rebuilt on French ground. Poland itself has no territory.
suggested_refs: The Polish équipe Z under French command, autumn 1939

stops.name: Gretz-Armainvilliers, the Château de Vignolles: P.C. Bruno
stops.date_confidence: attested to 20 October 1939 (Wikipedia, 'Marian Rejewski'). Coordinate corrected: the pool gave 48.7736/2.7300, about 3.6 km north of the commune; OSM places Gretz-Armainvilliers at 48.7410/2.7360. Wikipedia's 'PC Bruno' article says the chateau lay some forty kilometres southeast of Paris, not east as the pool's note had it. No P.C. Bruno pin previously existed anywhere in the corpus.
stops.campa: The équipe Z is installed in the Château de Vignolles at Gretz-Armainvilliers, some forty kilometres southeast of Paris, and the station is named Bruno. A teleprinter cable runs between Bruno and Bletchley Park, and the traffic passing along it is enciphered on Enigma doubles. Rejewski works keys with the perforated sheets, Zygalski's design, which Bletchley has now cut in quantity on machinery Poland never had. He is at the chateau from October 1939 to the following June.
suggested_refs: The Château de Vignolles at Gretz-Armainvilliers, station P.C. Bruno, 1939-1940

stops.name: Gretz-Armainvilliers, the visitor from Bletchley
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1940 by GCHQ, 'The Pyry Forest Meeting', which states that Turing's conversations with Rejewski were fundamental to the design of the first British bombe; no reached source gives the day, so it defaults to 01. Wikipedia's 'PC Bruno' article does not mention the visit, and the claim that Bruno recovered its first wartime key on 17 January 1940 could not be confirmed and is omitted. alan_turing.journey.json carries no stop for this visit.
stops.campa: Alan Turing comes over from Bletchley Park in January and spends time at the chateau. He talks with Rejewski about the machine, about plugboard connections, about what the Poles did and about the exact point where it stopped working in September 1938. He goes back with the perforated-sheet method and with the shape of a device that will become the British bombe, a different animal from the Polish bomba and descended from it. GCHQ's own account puts those conversations at the root of the first British machine. Rejewski is thirty-four; Turing is twenty-seven.
stops.quote: Turing's conversations with Marian Rejewski, the Polish mathematician and cryptanalyst were fundamental to developing the thinking which led to the design and installation of the first British 'Bombe'...
suggested_refs: Turing's January 1940 visit to P.C. Bruno
alan_turing.journey.json, which records no stop for the Bruno visit

stops.name: Oran, the summer of the armistice
stops.date_confidence: attested to 24 June 1940 for the evacuation by air to Algeria (Wikipedia, 'Marian Rejewski'); marian-rejewski.pl places him in or near Oran through the summer. The southward road through La Ferté, Vensant, Larche, Agen and Toulouse is from the same chronology and is compressed into this stop rather than given pins of its own.
stops.campa: France falls, and Bruno evacuates south by road through La Ferté, Vensant, Larche, Agen and Toulouse, and then out of the collapsing country by air. Rejewski spends the summer near Oran, in a French colony under an armistice government, cut off from Poland, from Britain and from the work. Bertrand is meanwhile negotiating with Vichy for leave to restart a cryptology station on French soil, under a cover, without informing the Germans that it exists.
suggested_refs: The evacuation of P.C. Bruno to Algeria, June 1940

stops.name: Uzès, the Château des Fouzes: P.C. Cadix
stops.date_confidence: attested: return to Marseille with false papers on 26 September 1940 and the opening of Cadix on 1 October 1940 (marian-rejewski.pl; en.wikipedia). This corrects the pool's chronology entry of '1940-09'. The cover name is given as 'Pierre Ranaud, a lycee professor from Nantes' by Wikipedia and spelled 'Pierre Raneau' by the museum chronology. Coordinate corrected to OSM's Château des Fouzes, Route de Bagnols-sur-Cèze, Uzès, 44.0216/4.4343.
stops.campa: He lands at Marseille on the twenty-sixth of September carrying papers in the name of Pierre Ranaud, a lycee professor from Nantes, and on the first of October the station opens in the Château des Fouzes outside Uzès in the Gard. Its cover is Travaux Ruraux, an agricultural survey office. Fifteen Poles and seven Spaniards read German and Soviet traffic from a country house in the unoccupied zone for two years. German direction-finding vans work the roads of the south of France throughout.
suggested_refs: The Château des Fouzes near Uzès, station P.C. Cadix, 1940-1942
The Travaux Ruraux cover organisation

stops.name: Château des Fouzes, the news from the Lamoricière
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia confirms that Różycki died in the sinking of a French passenger ship on 9 January 1942, returning from Algeria to Cadix. The ship's name, the Lamoricière, and the co-victims Graliński and Smoleński are standard in the literature and were not confirmed against a primary source this session. The stop sits at Cadix, where Rejewski was, not at the sinking.
stops.campa: Word reaches Cadix that the Lamoricière has gone down in the Mediterranean on the crossing from Algiers. Jerzy Różycki is aboard, on the return leg of a posting to the Algerian outstation, with Jan Graliński and Piotr Smoleński. Różycki is thirty-two years old. He had been in the locked room in Poznań in 1929, at the desk in Warsaw through the whole of 1932, and in the forest at Pyry in July 1939, and he is the first of the three to die. How Rejewski took the news, or from whom, is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The sinking of the Lamoricière, 9 January 1942
Marek Grajek, 'Mysteries of P.C. Cadix and its Evacuation in 1942/43'

stops.name: Uzès, the station scattered
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1942 for the dispersal of Cadix as German forces entered the unoccupied zone (marian-rejewski.pl; Wikipedia); no reached source gives the day, and the 9th is a placeholder within the attested month. The eleven weeks of safe addresses before the Pyrenees crossing is an inference from the dispersal date and the 29 January 1943 arrest.
stops.campa: German forces move into the unoccupied zone and Cadix closes and scatters within hours. Rejewski and Zygalski go south on false papers, through Nice and Cannes and Toulouse, hunted now in a country where they have no legal existence and no consulate to walk into. Bertrand's people keep them moving between safe addresses for eleven weeks. The plan is Spain, then Portugal, then Britain, and the first stage of it is a paid guide over the Pyrenees in January.
suggested_refs: The German occupation of the Vichy zone, November 1942, and the dispersal of the Cadix personnel

segments.name: The Pyrenees, and the Rank of Private

stops.name: Puigcerdà, the guide with the pistol
stops.date_confidence: attested to 29 January 1943 (Wikipedia, 'Marian Rejewski'; marian-rejewski.pl), including the robbery by the guide and the arrest by Spanish police near Puigcerdà. That Spain interned Polish escapers in large numbers is general context and is not sourced to a document here.
stops.campa: They cross the mountains on foot at night behind a paid guide, and a few hundred metres past the border the guide takes out a pistol and robs them of everything they are carrying. Rejewski is thirty-seven and carries in his head the wiring of the German Enigma, the design of the bomba and the whole of what Bruno and Cadix read. Spanish police pick him and Zygalski up shortly afterwards near Puigcerdà and book them as undocumented foreigners under whatever names they give. Spain is neutral, on friendly terms with Berlin, and interning Poles by the thousand.
suggested_refs: The January 1943 Pyrenees crossing of Rejewski and Zygalski

stops.name: Lleida, the prisons of the Cerdanya and the plain
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sequence of Spanish detentions, Bellver then Seo de Urgel then Lleida, from marian-rejewski.pl, which also records the rheumatism; day within March is a placeholder, since the chronology gives only March to May at Lleida. The Polish Red Cross and diplomatic intervention is attested by Wikipedia without detail.
stops.campa: The Spanish move them from Puigcerdà to Bellver, from Bellver to Seo de Urgel, from Seo de Urgel to the prison at Lleida: unheated cells through a wet winter on the ordinary prison ration. He comes out of it with rheumatism that he keeps for the rest of his life. Nobody in any of those buildings knows who he is, and it is essential that nobody find out, which is the only protection he has. The Polish Red Cross and the London government's embassy in Madrid work at the case from outside for three months.
suggested_refs: Spanish internment of Polish escapers, 1943

stops.name: Madrid, the months of waiting
stops.date_confidence: contradiction not resolved: most sources give 4 May 1943 for the release, one competing chronology gives 24 May, and the pool could not adjudicate. Wikipedia and marian-rejewski.pl agree that he then went to Madrid and stayed until July.
stops.campa: Released in May, he waits in Madrid through the late spring and into July for the arrangements that will move him on: a Polish officer without a uniform, in the capital of a state on friendly terms with Germany. He has been out of cryptologic work for six months by now, and will be out of it, in the sense that matters, for good. What he does with those weeks is not recorded anywhere. From Madrid the route runs through Portugal and down to Gibraltar.
suggested_refs: Polish evacuation routes through Spain and Portugal, 1943

stops.name: Hendon, London: arrival by air
stops.date_confidence: contradiction not resolved: marian-rejewski.pl gives 30 July 1943 for the Hendon landing, Wikipedia gives 3 August 1943; the pool could not settle which. The 3rd is used and the discrepancy is left standing. That he was inducted as a private on 16 August is attested (Wikipedia). That nobody from Bletchley Park sought him out is the consistent account of the literature and is an argument from silence.
stops.campa: By sea from Gibraltar and then by air, he lands at Hendon in north London in the first days of August, four years after leaving Warsaw and three and a half after the last time he touched Enigma traffic that mattered. Bletchley Park by now runs at industrial scale, with bombes in halls and thousands of staff, and it does not send for him. He is taken into the Polish Armed Forces in Britain on the sixteenth of August, his thirty-eighth birthday, and given the rank of private.
suggested_refs: RAF Hendon, arrival point of Polish personnel evacuated through Gibraltar

stops.name: Stanmore Park, the section designated N
stops.date_confidence: attested: second lieutenant 10 October 1943 (MacTutor), lieutenant 1 January 1945 (MacTutor), the Stanmore and Felden postings and the double Playfair work on SS and Sicherheitsdienst traffic (marian-rejewski.pl). Demobilisation date contradiction: Wikipedia gives discharge 15 November 1946 and return to Poland 21 November; MacTutor gives 21 November for the demobilisation itself.
stops.campa: Commissioned second lieutenant in October, he is put to work in the Polish signals establishment at Stanmore Park and at Felden near Boxmoor, heading the German section designated N: hand ciphers, the double Playfair used by the SS and the Sicherheitsdienst. It is competent work and it is not Enigma, which the British are running without him and will not discuss with an ally they have stopped sharing everything with. He makes lieutenant in January 1945 and is demobilised in November 1946.
suggested_refs: The Polish signals section N at Stanmore Park and Felden, 1943-1946

stops.name: Gdynia, the return by sea
stops.date_confidence: attested to 21 November 1946 (MacTutor; marian-rejewski.pl). That most of his colleagues remained in Britain and that Zygalski taught mathematics in England is general context from the literature and was not verified against a source this session [R].
stops.campa: He comes back by sea to Gdynia on the twenty-first of November, into a country with new borders, a new government, and a security service that treats every soldier returning from the West as a probable British agent. Most of the men he served with stay in England; Zygalski stays and teaches mathematics there for the rest of his life. Rejewski has a wife and two children in Bydgoszcz whom he has not seen since September 1939, and a lieutenant's discharge papers from an army the new state regards with suspicion. He goes home.
suggested_refs: Repatriation of Polish forces from Britain, 1946-1947

stops.name: Bydgoszcz, ul. Dworcowa 10: the reunion
stops.date_confidence: attested for the address ul. Dworcowa 10, flat 2, and the 21 November 1946 reunion (marian-rejewski.pl). Coordinate corrected from the pool's 53.1197/18.0027, about 770 m south, to OSM's geocode of ul. Dworcowa 10, 53.1266/18.0023. That no account of the reunion survives is a statement about the sources reached, not a claim that none exists anywhere.
stops.campa: Irena and the children have been living with her mother at ul. Dworcowa 10, flat 2, through the occupation and after it. Andrzej is ten and was three when his father left. Janina is seven and has never seen him. He does not tell them, then or at any point in the twenty years that follow, what he did before the war. The reunion falls on the twenty-first of November 1946, seven years and two months after the evacuation, and no account of it survives from either side.
suggested_refs: The flat at ul. Dworcowa 10/2, Bydgoszcz

stops.name: Bydgoszcz, the Kabel Polski works: the invoicing section
stops.date_confidence: attested from 1 February 1947 to the 1950 dismissal (marian-rejewski.pl). Sources disagree on the post: the museum chronology makes him head of the invoicing section, Wikipedia calls him director of sales. The security investigations of 1949-1958 and their negative result are attested by Wikipedia. Coordinate is an approximate Bydgoszcz placement; the factory's exact address was not confirmed.
stops.campa: He takes a post at the Kabel Polski cable works, running the invoicing section, a mathematician of the first rank doing arithmetic for a factory. The plant is classified as strategically important, which means the security service reviews its personnel, which means a man with a wartime record in the West and unexplained years in his file cannot remain there. He is forced out in 1950. Between 1949 and 1958 the Office of Public Security opens and reopens an investigation into him, and closes it each time without a finding.
suggested_refs: Kabel Polski, Bydgoszcz
Wojciech Polak's study of the Polish security files on Rejewski

stops.name: Bydgoszcz, the death of Andrzej
stops.date_confidence: attested to 9 July 1947 by marian-rejewski.pl, which gives the precise date; Wikipedia gives only 'summer 1947'. The museum chronology is followed here. The pin is the family address, not a confirmed place of death.
stops.campa: Andrzej Rejewski dies of complications of poliomyelitis on the ninth of July, eleven years old. His father has been home under eight months, out of the seven years the war took. There is no vaccine anywhere in the world; there will not be one for another eight years. The boy was three when his father left Warsaw and ten when he came back through Gdynia. Janina is eight and is now the only child. The boy is buried in Bydgoszcz, and his father goes back to the invoicing section of the cable works.
suggested_refs: Bydgoszcz burial records, July 1947

stops.name: Bydgoszcz, ul. Gdańska 10: the memoir written in longhand
stops.date_confidence: attested but disentangled from the pool, which conflated two events: marian-rejewski.pl gives the disability pension from 1 February 1967, the first memoir typescript in April 1967, and the move to ul. Gdańska 10 in the summer. The stop is dated to the summer move; month is attested, day defaults to 01. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 53.1189/18.0034 to OSM's ul. Gdańska 10, 53.1252/18.0034. A second memoir followed in 1974.
stops.campa: A disability pension begins in February and the accounting jobs end. He is sixty-one, and nobody has ever formally released him from the oath he swore in a locked room in Poznań in 1929. In April he sits down anyway and writes out in longhand an account of his work in the Cipher Bureau between 1930 and 1945, and hands it to the Military Historical Institute in Warsaw, which files it. A second account will follow in 1974. In the summer the family moves to ul. Gdańska 10.
suggested_refs: Rejewski's 1967 and 1974 memoir typescripts at the Military Historical Institute, Warsaw

stops.name: Warsaw, ul. Gdańska 2: the questions arrive
stops.date_confidence: attested to 23 June 1969 for the move and the Warsaw address ul. Gdańska 2 (marian-rejewski.pl). The pool had flagged this as a contradiction with the Bydgoszcz address on ul. Gdańska 10; it is not one, since the two streets are in different cities. Coordinate is OSM's placement of ul. Gdańska in Żoliborz/Marymont. Bertrand's 1973 memoir as the trigger of publicity is attested by Wikipedia; the description of press visits to the flat is from the Polish literature summarised in the pool [R].
stops.campa: He moves to Warsaw, to ul. Gdańska in Żoliborz, and lives with his daughter Janina, her husband and their son. In 1973 Gustave Bertrand publishes his memoir in Paris and names the Poles, and the story begins moving through the western press. Rejewski, who has spent forty years not saying it, spends his last seven answering questions about six equations in three unknowns. Much of what is appearing in English about the break is wrong, and he writes long letters correcting it.
suggested_refs: Gustave Bertrand, Enigma ou la plus grande énigme de la guerre 1939-1945 (Paris, 1973)

stops.name: Warsaw, the paper in Applicationes Mathematicae
stops.date_confidence: attested for the publication, Applicationes Mathematicae 16.4 (1980), 543-559 (MacTutor); no month is given for the issue, so month and day default to 01. Caveat on the first quotation below: MacTutor prints Rejewski's introduction with an acknowledged 'few changes to the English', so it is a lightly edited rendering, not an unmediated transcription; the pool could not reach an independent copy of the journal text to check the original wording.
stops.campa: In the last months of his life he publishes the mathematics itself, forty-eight years after doing it: the permutation-group argument, the six equations, the theorem on the product of transpositions, set out for readers who can follow the algebra. It is the first time the method appears anywhere as mathematics rather than as an anecdote about a war, and the paper says so in its own introduction. It runs to seventeen pages. It is his second published paper on any subject, and he is seventy-four years old.
stops.quote: It should be mentioned that the present paper is the first publication on the mathematical background on the Enigma cipher breaking.
stops.quote_source: Marian Rejewski, introduction to 'An Application of the Theory of Permutations in Breaking the Enigma Cipher', Applicationes Mathematicae 16.4 (1980), 543-559, as rendered on the MacTutor History of Mathematics biography page
suggested_refs: Marian Rejewski, 'An Application of the Theory of Permutations in Breaking the Enigma Cipher', Applicationes Mathematicae 16.4 (1980)

stops.name: Warsaw, the thirteenth of February
stops.date_confidence: attested to 13 February 1980, heart attack, aged 74 (MacTutor, cross-checked with Wikipedia). The pin is his Warsaw home address on ul. Gdańska; no source reached states where he died. The characterisation of how widely the name was known outside Poland in 1980 is an inference from the publication history, not a sourced claim.
stops.campa: He dies of a heart attack on the thirteenth of February, seventy-four years old. The Polish notices describe a retired official of Bydgoszcz who had been a mathematician. Outside Poland the name is known by then to a few hundred people at most, most of them at Bletchley Park reunions or among the small number of historians who had read Bertrand and Kozaczuk and understood what they were reading. He had been born a subject of the German Empire, in a town called Bromberg.
suggested_refs: Władysław Kozaczuk, W kręgu Enigmy (1979), the Polish account current at his death

stops.name: Powązki Military Cemetery, quarter B-39
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial with military honours in quarter B-39 (pl.wikipedia, giving the locator B39-4-3; marian-rejewski.pl). The funeral date is not given in any reached source and the stop carries the date of death. Coordinate reconciled: the pool held three different values for this one cemetery, 52.2528/20.9436, 52.2562/20.9502 and 52.2569/20.9614, two of which fall outside the walls; OSM's Cmentarz Wojskowy na Powązkach is 52.2586/20.9534. Irena's 1986 death and adjacent burial could not be verified by any source reached [R].
stops.campa: He is buried with military honours in quarter B-39 of the Powązki Military Cemetery, among the graves of the Warsaw Rising and the officers of the second republic. The rank on the stone is lieutenant, granted in Britain in 1945 for running a section that read SS hand ciphers, and not for anything done in the Saxon Palace, for which no rank exists in any army. The honours are those of the army of the Polish People's Republic, whose security service had opened files on him for a decade and closed them without a finding. Irena is laid beside him six years later.
suggested_refs: Quarter B-39, Cmentarz Wojskowy na Powązkach, Warsaw

stops.name: Powązki, the decree of the fourteenth of February
stops.date_confidence: contradiction resolved in favour of the primary document: pl.wikipedia quotes President Kwaśniewski's decree of 14 February 2000 with its Monitor Polski citation, M.P. 2000 nr 13, poz. 273; en.wikipedia's unsourced 21 July 2000 contradicts it and is not followed. The pin is the grave, not the chancellery where the decree was signed.
stops.campa: President Aleksander Kwaśniewski signs a decree conferring the Grand Cross of the Order of Polonia Restituta, posthumously and jointly, on Marian Rejewski, Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski. It is the second-highest decoration the Polish state can give, and it arrives twenty years after the last of the three had died. The decree names all three of them in a single sentence. One of them lies in this quarter; Zygalski died in England, and Różycki went down with the Lamoricière in 1942.
suggested_refs: Presidential decree of 14 February 2000, Monitor Polski 2000 nr 13, poz. 273
sources: pl.wikipedia, 'Marian Rejewski', quoting M.P. 2000 nr 13, poz. 273

stops.name: Poznań, the monument in front of the Imperial Castle
stops.date_confidence: attested to 10 November 2007, the seventy-fifth anniversary of the break (MacTutor; Wikipedia for the three-sided bronze form). The jury verdict quoted below belongs to the 2002 design competition, five years before the unveiling; the pool's source line had attached it to 2007. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 52.4058/16.9268 to OSM's Zamek Cesarski, Święty Marcin 80/82, 52.4080/16.9187, which is also the university pin used earlier in this file.
stops.campa: A three-sided bronze prism is unveiled in front of the Imperial Castle in Poznań, in the city where the three of them were students, on the seventy-fifth anniversary of the break. It carries their names and no figures. It stands on the ground of the university where all three of them enrolled as students of mathematics. The competition jury of 2002 had chosen a design in which the sculptor stepped out of the way and left the mathematics standing alone. Rejewski said all his life that the work had been the first-year syllabus, applied.
stops.quote: ...represents in the purest form the brilliant thought of the three mathematicians. The artist himself seems to step aside permitting the spectator to contemplate the purely intellectual achievement of the three cryptologists.
stops.quote_source: Competition jury verdict (2002) on the winning design for the Poznań monument to Rejewski, Różycki and Zygalski, unveiled 10 November 2007, quoted on the MacTutor History of Mathematics biography page
suggested_refs: The Poznań Cryptologists Monument, Zamek Cesarski, unveiled 10 November 2007

stops.name: Poznań, the memoir printed at last
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2011 for the first book publication, with a second edition in 2013, by the Adam Mickiewicz University Press edition page; no month is given, so month and day default to 01. A shorter first appearance of the same typescripts ran in Przegląd Historyczno-Wojskowy 6 (2005), special no. 5, pp. 71-204, per the AMU bibliographic record. Coordinate is OSM's Collegium Martineum, Poznań; the Enigma Cipher Centre opened in that building on 24 September 2021, a day-date resting on the AMU press release alone.
stops.campa: The handwritten memoirs of 1967 and 1974, held by the Military Historical Institute for four decades, are printed together as a book for the first time by the Adam Mickiewicz University Press, in Polish and English on facing pages. A shorter version of the same typescripts had run in a military history journal in 2005. Ten years after the book, the university opens an Enigma Cipher Centre in the Collegium Martineum, a few streets from the lecture rooms where Krygowski taught him permutations.
stops.quote: Wiele teraz hałasu wokół naszego złamania Enigmy. A myśmy przecież nie zrobili nic poza zastosowaniem wiedzy, którą na pierwszym roku studiów przekazali nam Krygowski i Abramowicz.
stops.quote_source: Marian Rejewski, letter quoted in the editors' apparatus of Wspomnienia z mej pracy w Biurze Szyfrów Oddziału II Sztabu Głównego w latach 1930-1945, Adam Mickiewicz University Press (no official published English translation was located)
suggested_refs: Wspomnienia z mej pracy w Biurze Szyfrów / Memories of My Work at the Cipher Bureau, AMU Press, 2011 and 2013
The Enigma Cipher Centre, Collegium Martineum, Poznań
sources: Adam Mickiewicz University Press, edition page for Rejewski's Wspomnienia

stops.name: Bydgoszcz Główna, the station takes his name
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R] as to the ceremony: the gov.pl page reporting it, 'Kryptolog Marian Rejewski patronem dworca kolejowego Bydgoszcz Główna', did not resolve on refetch, so the 2 February 2022 date, the ranking as the ninth station named under the PKP programme and the attendee list are unconfirmed. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 53.1223/18.0114, which pointed at the city centre 2.1 km away, to OSM's Bydgoszcz Główna, 7 Zygmunta Augusta, 53.1353/17.9916. The 2005 bench, by Michał Kubiak per Wikipedia, and the 2017 mural 'Odszyfrowany Rejewski' by Juliusz Nowicki are both attested by Wikipedia.
stops.campa: The main railway station of Bydgoszcz is given Marian Rejewski as its patron, with a plaque and a ceremony. In the same town there is a bench with his bronze figure sitting on it, put up in 2005 for the centenary of his birth. He had left this town in 1923 with a gymnasium certificate and come back in 1946 to work out invoices for a cable factory. On the wall of the building on Gdańska Street where he lived from 1967 there is a mural, painted in 2017, titled Odszyfrowany Rejewski, Rejewski Decrypted.
suggested_refs: Bydgoszcz Główna station, patron ceremony of February 2022
Michał Kubiak's 2005 bench memorial and Juliusz Nowicki's 2017 mural, Bydgoszcz
